## Background

Butterflies in the Danaini tribe primarily use milkweeds (Apocynaceae) as host plants. Within the tribe, the monarch butterfly (*Danaus plexippus*) is particularly well known for its specialization on milkweeds in the genus *Asclepias* (Asclepiadoideae, Apocynaceae), which produce cardiac glycoside toxins known as cardenolides. Resistance to cardenolides is mediated by target-site insensitivity of the Na⁺,K⁺-ATPase α-subunit (ATPα), which evolved stepwise along the monarch lineage through amino acid substitutions at positions 111, 119, and 122, generating three levels of resistance ([Petschenka et al., 2013](https://academic.oup.com/evolut/article/67/9/2753/6851605); [Karageorgi et al., 2019](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1610-8)).

The goal of this analysis was to test the functional consequences of these substitutions by measuring survival on Asclepias diets spanning a gradient of cardenolide defenses, using engineered *Drosophila melanogaster* lines carrying reconstructed ATPα genotypes representing three levels of target-site insensitivity in Danaini, together with two outgroup genotypes.

We selected six Asclepias species known to serve as monarch hosts and spanning a broad range of cardenolide defenses ([Rasmann et al., 2011](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1461-0248.2011.01609.x)). Cardenolide defense varies along three main axes: total cardenolide concentration, diversity of cardenolide compounds, and polarity, with more non-polar compounds generally considered more toxic. Rasmann et al. (2011) showed that these axes are correlated: species with higher constitutive cardenolide concentrations also tend to produce a greater diversity of cardenolides, more non-polar compounds, and stronger induction following monarch caterpillar attack.

In addition, we added another non-native monarch host plant from a sister genus, Gomphocarpus physocarpus, which has been reported to have intermediate foliar cardenolide leves with A. curassavica ([Friedman et al., 2020](https://academic.oup.com/evolut/article/74/2/377/6726937)).

In 2020, we grew and harvested seven milkweed species spanning a range of cardenolide concentrations as a proxy for the broader range of cardenolide defense: *A. tuberosa, A. syriaca, A. viridis, A. curassavica, A. perennis,* and *A. asperula* ([Rasmann et al., 2011](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1461-0248.2011.01609.x)), as well as *G. physocarpus*. We dried and pulverized the harvested foliar tissue for use in bioassays.

In the bioassays, we measured larval-to-adult survival of engineered *D. melanogaster* lines carrying ATPα genotypes observed along the lineage leading to the monarch butterfly (QAN, QSN, LAN, LSN, VSN, VSH) on either control medium (20% lettuce powder, no plant powder) or medium supplemented with 20% milkweed or *Gomphocarpus* leaf powder. Each genotype was tested in 1–4 trials, with 30 larvae per trial.

## Data

### 1. Bioassay data

Conducted by Naama Weksler (import & clean)

The first step in the analysis was to import and clean the data. It was previously organized into tidy data files, with one file for each independent replicate. I imported these files and then removed lines for which there was an N/A indicating that the experiment wasn't done. I then combined the four independent data frames into one, with an additional column indicating which replicate they originated from.

```{r, scroll_output = TRUE}
replicate_1 <- read.csv("./data/Experiment_1_OCT2020.csv")
replicate_2 <- read.csv("./data/Experiment_2_NOV2020.csv")
replicate_3 <- read.csv("./data/Experiment_3_NOV2020.csv")
replicate_4 <- read.csv("./data/Experiment_4_NOV2020.csv")

combined <- bind_rows(
  replicate_1 %>% mutate(replicate = "rep1"),
  replicate_2 %>% mutate(replicate = "rep2"),
  replicate_3 %>% mutate(replicate = "rep3"),
  replicate_4 %>% mutate(replicate = "rep4")
)

#this cleans the data
combined_clean <- combined %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  filter(Pupae != "N/A") %>% 
  dplyr::rename(media = Media, genotype = Genotype, date = Counting.Day, vial = Vial, pupae = Pupae, 
         adults = Adults, verification = Verification, input = Input, dev_day = Developmental.Day) %>%
  dplyr::select(media, genotype, date, vial, pupae, adults, dev_day, replicate) %>% mutate(adults = as.numeric(adults), 
                                                                                    pupae = as.numeric(pupae)) %>%
  mutate(media = str_trim(media))

plants_represented <- unique(combined_clean$media)

combined %>% gt()
```

### 2. Milkweed cardenolide defense data

Conducted by Naama Weksler (import & clean)

I pulled the milkweed cardenolide defense data (concentration, diversity, and polarity) from [Rasmann et al., 2011](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1461-0248.2011.01609.x).

```{r}
plant_toxicity_raw = read.csv("./data/ra_2011_supp_data.csv")
plant_toxicity = plant_toxicity_raw %>% filter(organ == "S") %>% dplyr::select(-nodes, -latitude)
plant_toxicity$species = str_remove(plant_toxicity$species, "^.\\.\\s")

plants_represented = setdiff(unique(combined_clean$media), "physocarpus")

plant_toxicity_filtered = plant_toxicity %>% 
  filter(species %in% plants_represented)

plant_toxicity_filtered %>% gt()
```

### 3. Combined data

```{r}
# make a pivot table summarizing the total number of adults and pupae observed
# also correct values above 30 to 30
combined_pivot = combined_clean %>%
  filter(media != "physocarpus") %>%
  group_by(vial, media, genotype, replicate) %>%
  summarise(
    pupae = sum(pupae, na.rm = TRUE),
    adults = sum(adults, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    pupae = if_else(pupae > 30, 30, pupae),
    adults = if_else(adults > 30, 30, adults)
  )

# combine the pivot table with the plant toxicity table
pivot_plant_vals = left_join(
  combined_pivot,
  plant_toxicity_filtered,
  by = c("media" = "species")
)

# add values for control and lettuce media
pivot_plant_vals = pivot_plant_vals %>%
  mutate(
    total_conc = if_else(media %in% c("control", "lettuce"), 0, total_conc),
    num_peaks = if_else(media %in% c("control", "lettuce"), 0, num_peaks),
    diversity = if_else(media %in% c("control", "lettuce"), 0, diversity),
    polarity = if_else(media %in% c("control", "lettuce"), NA_real_, polarity)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(-any_of("organ")) %>%
  filter(genotype != "QSN")
```

```{r, scroll_output = TRUE}
#add success / failure columns ("emerge" vs. "not emerge"), cardenolide containing, and remove extraneous information
data_clean <- pivot_plant_vals %>% 
  mutate(
    emerge = adults,
    not_emerge = 30 - adults,
    percent_survival = (emerge / 30) * 100,
    media = factor(media, levels = c(
      "control", "lettuce", "tuberosa", "syriaca",
      "viridis", "curassavica", "perennis", "asperula"
    )),
    genotype = factor(genotype, levels = c("QAN", "LAN", "LSN", "VSN", "VSH")),
    media_type = ifelse(media %in% c("control", "lettuce"),
                        "Control diets",
                        "Cardenolide−containing Asclepias diets"),
    media_type = factor(media_type, levels = c("Control diets", "Cardenolide−containing Asclepias diets"))
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(-num_peaks, -pupae)


data_clean = data_clean %>%
  mutate(media_type = ifelse(media %in% c("control", "lettuce"), 
                              "Control diets", 
                              "Cardenolide−containing Asclepias diets"))

data_clean %>% gt()
```

## Statistics

### 1. Genotype comparison for toxic/non-toxic media

From the exploratory analysis, it is obvious that there are differences in survival across different genotypes on different milkweed-containing media. We first asked whether VSH confers a survival advantage on toxic plants relative to each of the other genotypes, compared to control media.

```{r}
#create a variable distinguishing toxic vs non-toxic media
data_clean = data_clean %>%
  mutate(
    media_type = ifelse(
      media %in% c("control", "lettuce"),
      "Control diets",
      "Cardenolide-containing Asclepias diets"
    ),
    media_type = factor(
      media_type,
      levels = c("Control diets", "Cardenolide-containing Asclepias diets")
    ),
    genotype = factor(
      genotype,
      levels = c("QAN", "LAN", "LSN", "VSN", "VSH")
    )
  )

# Fit model with media_type
model1 = glm(
  cbind(emerge, not_emerge) ~ genotype * media_type,
  data = data_clean,
  family = quasibinomial
)

round(summary(model1)$dispersion, 2)

tbl_coef <- tidy(model1, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) %>%   # ORs for binomial/logit
  mutate(across(c(estimate, conf.low, conf.high, std.error, statistic, p.value),
                ~round(.x, 3)))

kable(tbl_coef, caption = "GLM (logit) coefficients reported as odds ratios")
```

<br> The model shows that VSH genotype does have a significant effect on survival on toxic media compared to control, when compared to all other genotypes with a multiple hypothesis testing correction.

```{r}
### Predicted means & SE
#get estimated marginal means
emm = emmeans(model1, ~ genotype*media_type, type = "response")

#save as data frame for plotting
emm_df = as.data.frame(emm)
```

```{r, scroll_output = TRUE}
# Get ALL pairwise comparisons of genotypes within each media type
all_comparisons = pairs(emm, simple = "genotype", adjust = "bonferroni")

# View results as a data frame
all_comparisons_df = as.data.frame(all_comparisons)%>%
  mutate(significant = ifelse(p.value < 0.05, "Yes", "No"))

kable(all_comparisons)
```

### 2.1 Genotype comparison for individual media types

While it's an interesting result that VSH provides resistance to toxic media, by looking at the graph it seems likely that this effect is driven strongly by the large difference in survival on media containing milkweed with the highest chemical defenses. *A. asperula* and *A. perennis* contain the highest concentration of cardenolides in our panel.

Thus, we continued the analysis by probing whether different fly lines had significantly different survival on individual media with different defenses, rather than grouped toxic vs. non-toxic conditions. One note here is that due to the relatively low sample size, we did not have high power for this analysis.

As before, we fit a generalized linear model to the data. However, in this analysis we used media, rather than media type, as the predictor variable. As in [Karageorgi et al., 2019](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1610-8), we compared marginal means in a pairwise manner to calculate odds ratios and p values for each pair with a multiple hypothesis testing adjustment. This effectively compares each pair of genotypes of every single different media, testing whether their survival differed on that media. This ends up being a very large number of pairwise comparisons, but nonetheless some of them are significant. Note that 100% of significant pairwise differences involve VSH, and most of them occur on highly toxic milkweed media. On the milkweed species with the highest cardenolide concentration, *A. asperula*, survival of VSH flies significantly differs from that of all four other genotypes.

```{r, scroll_output = TRUE}
# Fit model with media
model2 = glm(
  cbind(emerge, not_emerge) ~ genotype*media,
  data = data_clean,
  family = quasibinomial
)

summary(model2)

round(summary(model2)$dispersion, 2)


### Predicted means & SE
# Estimated marginal means for each genotype within each medium
emm2 = emmeans(model2, ~ genotype | media, type = "response")
emm2

# All pairwise comparisons of genotypes within each medium
all_comparisons2 = pairs(emm2, by = "media", adjust = "bonferroni")

all_comparisons_df2 = as.data.frame(all_comparisons2) %>%
  mutate(significant = if_else(p.value < 0.05, "Yes", "No")) %>%
  arrange(p.value)


table_s2c = all_comparisons_df2 %>%
  mutate(
    media = factor(
      media,
      levels = c("control", "lettuce", "tuberosa", "syriaca",
                 "viridis", "curassavica", "perennis", "asperula")
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(media, contrast) %>%
  transmute(
    Diet = case_when(
      media == "control" ~ "Control",
      media == "lettuce" ~ "Lettuce",
      media == "tuberosa" ~ "A. tuberosa",
      media == "syriaca" ~ "A. syriaca",
      media == "viridis" ~ "A. viridis",
      media == "curassavica" ~ "A. curassavica",
      media == "perennis" ~ "A. perennis",
      media == "asperula" ~ "A. asperula"
    ),
    Contrast = contrast,
    `Odds ratio` = case_when(
      odds.ratio < 0.001 ~ formatC(odds.ratio, format = "e", digits = 2),
      odds.ratio > 1000 ~ formatC(odds.ratio, format = "e", digits = 2),
      TRUE ~ sprintf("%.3f", odds.ratio)
    ),
    SE = case_when(
      SE < 0.001 ~ formatC(SE, format = "e", digits = 2),
      SE > 1000 ~ formatC(SE, format = "e", digits = 2),
      TRUE ~ sprintf("%.3f", SE)
    ),
    `z ratio` = sprintf("%.3f", z.ratio),
    `Bonferroni-adjusted p-value` = case_when(
      p.value < 0.001 ~ "<0.001",
      TRUE ~ sprintf("%.3f", p.value)
    )
  )

table_s2c

vsh_comparisons_only = all_comparisons_df2 %>%
  dplyr::filter(stringr::str_detect(contrast, "VSH"))

all_comparisons_df2 %>% gt()
```

Letters per genotype within each medium for plot 1 - the letter show in a compact way which genotypes are the same and which are different

```{r}
# Compact letter display per medium (based on same model & contrasts)
cld2 = cld(
  emm2,
  by      = "media",
  adjust  = "bonferroni",  # same correction as in pairs()
  Letters = letters,
  type    = "response"
)

letters_df = cld2 %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    media    = factor(media, levels = levels(data_clean$media)),
    genotype = factor(genotype, levels = c("QAN","LAN","LSN","VSN","VSH")),
    letters  = stringr::str_trim(.group)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(media, genotype, letters)
```

### 3.1 Genotype comparison across axes of cardenolide defense

We also asked how variation in milkweed chemical defense correlated with survival across genotypes. In selecting milkweed species, we used cardenolide concentration as a proxy for defenses ([Rasmann et al., 2011](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1461-0248.2011.01609.x)). However, cardenolide defense varies along three main axes: total cardenolide concentration, diversity of cardenolide compounds, and polarity, with more non-polar compounds generally considered more toxic. These axes are correlated, such that species with higher constitutive cardenolide concentrations also tend to produce a greater diversity of cardenolides and more non-polar compounds.

As expected, in the species we selected cardenolide concentration, diversity and polarity are all positively correlated. This makes the use of the 3 axes of cardenolide defense not optimal to use as predictors in a regression model because it complicates the estimation of individual effects within the [model](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/machine-learning/multicollinearity-in-regression-analysis/).

```{r}
# collinearity test
cor(data_clean[, c("total_conc", "diversity", "polarity")], use = "complete.obs")
```

Nevertheless, we fitted a full model including cardenolide concentration, diversity, and polarity to ask how survival varied across the multidimensional cardenolide defense axes.

```{r}
model_full <- glm(
  cbind(emerge, not_emerge) ~ genotype * (total_conc + diversity + polarity),
  family = quasibinomial(),
  data = data_clean
)

summary(model_full)

# check for variance inflation
vif(model_full)
```

Variance inflation was high in the full multivariate interaction model, indicating substantial collinearity among predictors and their genotype-specific effects, which limited interpretation of individual coefficient estimates. We therefore focused our subsequent analysis on total cardenolide concentration as a representative and biologically interpretable measure of host-plant chemical defense.

In this analysis, we modeled survival for each vial as a binomial outcome (adults "successes" out of larvae "trials") using a logistic regression with a quasibinomial family to accommodate overdispersion. We linked the survival probability (p) to predictors via the logit, (\log{p/(1-p)} = \beta\_0 + \beta\_1,\text{total_conc} + \beta\_2,\text{genotype} + \beta\_3,(\text{total_conc} \times \text{genotype})). We interpreted the slope for a genotype as the change in log-odds of survival per one-unit increase in dose (total_conc), which quantified that line's sensitivity to toxicity. To identify which genotypes differed, we used emtrends to obtain model-adjusted (marginal) slopes for each genotype and then compared them with pairwise contrasts, as well as a focused contrast of VSH versus the mean of all other genotypes.

```{r}
# fit logistic: adults successes out of larvae trials; allowing genotype-specific slopes
model3 = glm(
  cbind(emerge, not_emerge) ~ total_conc * genotype,
  family = quasibinomial(),
  data = data_clean
)

# model summary
summary(model3)

# dispersion parameter (phi), rounded to 2 decimals
round(summary(model3)$dispersion, 2)

# estimated slopes (on logit scale) per genotype
slopes = emtrends(model3, specs = "genotype", var = "total_conc")
slopes
# genotype-specific slopes (Tukey-adjusted if you want to test each slope against 0)
slope_tests = summary(slopes, infer = c(TRUE, TRUE), adjust = "tukey") %>%
  as.data.frame()

kable(slope_tests)

# # pairwise slope differences among genotypes (Tukey-adjusted)
# pairwise_slopes = pairs(slopes, adjust = "tukey") %>%
#   as.data.frame()
# 
# kable(pairwise_slopes)

# compare VSH from the other genotypes
vsh_vs_others = contrast(
  slopes,
  method = "trt.vs.ctrlk",   # compares each genotype to the last one = VSH
  adjust = "bonferroni"
) %>%
  as.data.frame()

kable(vsh_vs_others)
```

From the global contrast, we can observe that the only genotype with a significantly different slope from the others is VSH, with a p value of 0.04.

```{r}
# full slope summary per genotype
sl_raw = summary(slopes, infer = c(TRUE, TRUE)) %>%
  as_tibble()

# find the slope column automatically
trend_col = grep("\\.trend$", names(sl_raw), value = TRUE)

sl_df = sl_raw %>%
  mutate(
    slope = .data[[trend_col]],
    z = dplyr::coalesce(.data[["z.ratio"]], slope / SE),
    p = dplyr::coalesce(.data[["p.value"]], 2 * pnorm(abs(z), lower.tail = FALSE)),
    conf.low = dplyr::coalesce(.data[["asymp.LCL"]]),
    conf.high = dplyr::coalesce(.data[["asymp.UCL"]])
  ) %>%
  transmute(
    genotype,
    slope,
    SE,
    df,
    z = as.numeric(z),
    p = as.numeric(p),
    conf.low,
    conf.high
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2)))

sl_df %>% gt()
```

### 3.2 Plot genotype comparison/axes of cardenolide defense

```{r}

legend_order = c("QAN", "LAN", "LSN", "VSN", "VSH")

color_map = c("VSH" = "#c43240","VSN" = "#f4a261","QAN" = "#264653","LSN" = "#e9c46a","LAN" = "#287271")

# Convert genotype to a factor so ggplot uses the order above
data_clean$genotype = factor(data_clean$genotype, levels = legend_order)

# Convert percent_survival from 0–100 to 0–1 so it matches the model predictions from plogis()
plot_data = data_clean %>%
  mutate(percent_survival = percent_survival / 100)

# Create a grid of x-values across the observed range of total_conc
# for every genotype, so we can draw smooth prediction curves
pred_grid = expand.grid(
  total_conc = seq(
    min(plot_data$total_conc, na.rm = TRUE),   # minimum observed concentration
    max(plot_data$total_conc, na.rm = TRUE),   # maximum observed concentration
    length.out = 200                           # number of points for smooth lines
  ),
  genotype = legend_order
)

# Again force genotype to have the same factor order
pred_grid$genotype = factor(pred_grid$genotype, levels = legend_order)

# Predict from model3 on the link scale (logit scale) and also standard errors for confidence intervals
pred = predict(model3, newdata = pred_grid, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)

# Convert fitted values from logit scale to probability scale (0–1)
pred_grid$fit = plogis(pred$fit)

# Lower 95% CI bound, back-transformed to probability scale
pred_grid$lwr = plogis(pred$fit - 1.96 * pred$se.fit)

# Upper 95% CI bound, back-transformed to probability scale
pred_grid$upr = plogis(pred$fit + 1.96 * pred$se.fit)

# Build the plot
plot2 = ggplot() +

  # Add confidence ribbons from model3 predictions
  geom_ribbon(
    data = pred_grid,
    aes(
      x = total_conc,
      ymin = lwr,
      ymax = upr,
      fill = genotype,
      group = genotype
    ),
    alpha = 0.1
  ) +

  # Add fitted prediction lines from model3
  geom_line(
    data = pred_grid,
    aes(
      x = total_conc,
      y = fit,
      color = genotype,
      group = genotype
    ),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +

  # Add the raw observed data points
  geom_point(
    data = plot_data,
    aes(
      x = total_conc,
      y = percent_survival,
      color = genotype
    ),
    size = 1.5,
    alpha = 0.35,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +

  # Apply the manual color palette to lines and points
  scale_color_manual(
    values = color_map,
    breaks = legend_order,
    name = "Genotype",
    guide = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)
  ) +

  # Apply the same colors to ribbons, but suppress a separate fill legend
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = color_map,
    guide = "none"
  ) +

  # Set the y-axis to 0–1 because both points and predictions are now on the probability scale
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1),
    breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.03))
  ) +

  # Axis labels
  labs(
    x = "Cardenolide content (mg/g)",
    y = "Larval to adult survival (%)"
  ) +

  theme_classic(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.position = "none",   # legend hidden
    plot.title = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5),
    axis.line = element_line(linewidth = 0.25),
    axis.ticks = element_line(linewidth = 0.25)
  )

plot2

# Save the plot as a PDF
ggsave("./plots/plot2.pdf", plot = plot2, width = 8, height = 5)
```

### 4.1 Ggomph vs Acura comparison

```{r}
# ----------------------------
# keep only A. curassavica and G. physocarpus
# ----------------------------
data_ed2 = combined_clean %>%
  group_by(vial, media, genotype, replicate) %>%
  summarise(
    pupae = sum(pupae, na.rm = TRUE),
    adults = sum(adults, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    pupae = if_else(pupae > 30, 30, pupae),
    adults = if_else(adults > 30, 30, adults),
    emerge = adults,
    not_emerge = 30 - adults,
    percent_survival = (emerge / 30) * 100
  ) %>%
  filter(
    media %in% c("curassavica", "physocarpus"),
    genotype != "QSN"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    media = factor(media, levels = c("curassavica", "physocarpus")),
    genotype = factor(genotype, levels = c("QAN", "LAN", "LSN", "VSN", "VSH"))
  )
```

```{r}
model_ed2 = glm(
  cbind(emerge, not_emerge) ~ genotype * media,
  data = data_ed2,
  family = quasibinomial()
)

summary(model_ed2)
round(summary(model_ed2)$dispersion, 2)
```

```{r}
emm_ed2 = emmeans(model_ed2, ~ genotype | media, type = "response")

all_comparisons_ed2 = pairs(emm_ed2, by = "media", adjust = "bonferroni")

all_comparisons_ed2_df = as.data.frame(all_comparisons_ed2) %>%
  mutate(significant = if_else(p.value < 0.05, "Yes", "No"))

all_comparisons_ed2_df %>% gt()
```

```{r}
cld_ed2 = cld(
  emm_ed2,
  by = "media",
  adjust = "bonferroni",
  Letters = letters,
  type = "response"
)

letters_ed2 = cld_ed2 %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(
    media = factor(media, levels = c("curassavica", "physocarpus")),
    genotype = factor(genotype, levels = c("QAN", "LAN", "LSN", "VSN", "VSH")),
    letters = stringr::str_trim(.group)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(media, genotype, letters)
```
